This file holds tables and text removed from the main
paper to meet the page limit. Values are unchanged.
Table numbers refer to earlier drafts; cross-references and
citations shown as ?? point into the main paper.
I. Tables removed from the paper
II. Original eighteen limitations (full text, removed from
the paper)
We identify eighteen methodological limitations:
1) Absence of Licensed Legal Practitioner Evaluation
(Most Critical for Deployment): owing to geograph-
ical and institutional constraints, no licensed practi-
tioner evaluated the outputs. All faithfulness and
safety assessments rely on automated LLM-as-a-
judge scoring (Section ??) and ROUGE-L against
researcher-constructed references cross-referenced to
public sources (Cornell LII, Oyez, CRS Constitu-
tion Annotated). Dual-judge faithfulness correlates
only modestly with lexical grounding (Pearson r =
0.555, p =
1
10001 ≈9.999×10−5) and cannot replicate
practitioner judgment of legal correctness, tempo-
ral consistency, citation validity and hallucination.
Lacking a labeled validation set for the NLI Smart
Grader (Section ??), its false-non-entailment rate is
unquantified beyond ablation evidence. We consider
expert evaluation of output quality and verifier reli-
ability an essential prerequisite for deployment and
release the benchmark and code to invite replication.
The author spot-check in Section ?? is a single non-
expert review and no substitute.
2) Metric Disentanglement and Refusal-Volume Mask-
ing: aggregate faithfulness rewards non-committal
answers on unanswerable queries and can mask gen-
erative weaknesses. TERRA has the highest overall
(0.695 vs. 0.670; intervals overlap) and answer-only
faithfulness (0.586 vs. 0.392) with fewer flagged
refusals (139 vs. 165), but answer-only scores con-
dition on different answered subsets, and it leads
HippoRAG on Category B by +0.066 (q = 0.0124).
Benchmarks should report refusal rates alongside
answer-only faithfulness.
3) Score Ceiling and Rubric Granularity: 880 of the
1,750 canonical evaluations (50.3%) score exactly
1.0 under the five-point Likert rubric normalized
to [0, 1], which limits discrimination among high-
scoring systems.
4) Jurisdictional and Temporal Corpus Boundaries: the
EEG covers 20,000 U.S. Supreme Court opinions
spanning 1850–1980 in seven doctrinal domains
(Table ??); state, municipal, foreign and post-1980
law require further ingestion. Although Section ??
shows traversal stability under snapshot expansion
(T
→
T + N), live vector-index insertion and
streaming graph maintenance remain unaddressed.
5) Hosted API Output Variability at T = 0.0, Run-to-
Run Identity, and Sensitivity Verification: primary
evaluations used greedy decoding with databricks-
meta-llama-3-3-70b-instruct and databricks-gemma-
3-12b, but hosted APIs can vary across serving
sessions; query D066 shifted from EASY to HARD,
consistent with serving-level variability whose cause
cannot be isolated from the logs. Between two 14-
September TERRA executions, answers were string-
identical on 58.9% of queries (206/350): 95.0% on
Category A (95/100), 82.7% on C (62/75), 52.0% on
D (39/75) and 10.0% on B (10/100), with generation
and retrieval paths differing as documented. Both
were judged under the dual-judge protocol with the
frozen RAG prompt (SHA256: 6d18fc14…). A sensi-
tivity check with an 80B model (databricks-qwen3-
next-80b-a3b-instruct) on a separate 15-query subset
(10 Category B, 5 Category D) gave the same
ordering (no statistical test; not re-verified): TERRA
1.000 Category B faithfulness (Flat RAG 0.900,
Direct LLM 0.800) and 100% Category D safety
rejection (Flat RAG 40%, Direct LLM 0%). All anal-
yses are bound to SHA256-verified raw completion
archives; rerunning the endpoint may yield different
completions.

Pretraining

represented in pretraining corpora. On the discrete

Notes: Feature comparison distinguishing TERRA from generic RAG baselines and contemporary legal GraphRAG architectures.
Whereas LegalGraphRAG [?] and SAT-Graph RAG [?] model codified statutory provisions and formal legislative amendment events,
TERRA is specialized for longitudinal common-law precedent, where judicial authority evolves continuously through citation networks
and earlier precedents remain presumptive law unless explicitly modified or overruled. Furthermore, TERRA couples graph topology
directly with node-level procedural reasoning traces and an autonomous natural language inference (NLI) entailment gate to suppress
hallucinated endorsements of superseded doctrine.

14) Corpus Length-Filtering Bias and Concise Land-
mark Exclusion: the ≥4,000-character filter removes
noise (102,235 of 131,315 decisions in 399 volumes
are < 500 characters, 77.85%) but equates length
with authority: it excludes 8,324 decisions (500–
3,999 characters, 6.34%), 46 in the top 0.5% of
CAP PageRank. An audit of 63 landmarks finds
21 (33.33%) purged, including Haines (3,730 chars,
100.00th percentile), Diebold (2,441 chars, 100.00th),
Dusky (1,532 chars, 99.99th), Lucas v. Earl (3,654
chars), Sipuel (2,012 chars) and Gayle (712 chars);
Bolling v. Sharpe (5,137 chars) met the threshold but
was omitted in subsampling. Future graphs should
replace static floors with citation retention.
15) Citation Extraction Precision, Same-Year Chronol-
ogy, and Provenance Uncertainty: eyecite estab-
lishes citation existence, not doctrinal endorsement.
Our stratified audit (N
= 200, seed 20260924)
finds reporter strings in 100.0% of sampled edges
and verified direct reliance in 94.5% (95% CI:
[90.4%, 96.9%]), with 5.5% in quotations. 4,077 edges
(2.81%) link same-year opinions, with 13 intra-year
reversals from publication artifacts and zero cross-
year violations; the earlier “99.91% chronological
validity” claim was untraceable. Citation trails give
candidate authorities at 94.5% precision, not certi-
fied doctrinal paths.
16) Rule-Based Doctrinal Taxonomy, Lexical Polysemy,
Truncation, and Residual Fallback Bias: the seven-
domain classification uses a deterministic 69-phrase
lexicon over texts truncated to ≤4, 000 charac-
ters, so (1) keyword matching without disambigua-
tion can misclassify terms in dicta or dissents;
(2) truncation limits matching to introductory syl-
labi and can miss dispositive holdings; (3) the
general_constitutional_statutory fallback (4,594 de-
cisions, 22.97%) is a catch-all with 10.0% baseline
precision despite 100.00% validity as a residual class;
and (4) validation uses automated evaluators (raw
agreement 44.29%, κ = 0.3395) and an automated
adjudicator (34.15% weighted accuracy, 95% CI:
[25.27%, 43.02%]), not practitioner annotation, so
labels are not certified human ground truth.
17) A Priori Hyperparameter Selection and Sensitivity
Scope: retrieval and expansion parameters (k = 2,
d = 2, hub cap 50, τ = 1.30) were fixed before bench-
mark construction using topological constraints and
feasibility testing on an independent 35-query de-
velopment suite (August 2026). This guards against
test-set leakage but precludes claims of global opti-
mality. Sweeps over 22 configurations (Section ??,
Table ?? Panel C; k ∈{1, 2, 4}, d ∈{1, 2, 3},
C ∈{25, 50, 100}) show stability around the histor-
ical configuration (k = 2, d = 2, C = 50; 86.08%
macro recall, 62.0% full-path recall) and quantify
the coverage-eﬀiciency trade-off under operational
caps (90.85% landmark retention, 97.0% context
reduction).
18) Task-Corpus Domain Asymmetry and Private-Law
Generalizability: the index spans the full 20,000-
case docket (51.5% private and general statutory
law), but Category B evaluates constitutional and
public-law precedent only (100.0% across five public-
law domains; zero private-law chains). Performance
on the evaluated constitutional chains amid 5,707
private-law distractors does not extend to multi-

hop statutory or patent reasoning, which remains
unvalidated.
